config.motion: This house would adopt a nationwide four-day work week.

points: Wards on compressed four-day rota: burnout fell about a fifth, sleep improved, throughput stayed within normal variation.
Status quo costs: burnout rose 29% to 41%, nurses resigning at 14% a year, each replacement four months' salary.
Nationwide means statutory default with sectoral averaging and continuous-service exemptions, not identical schedules overnight.
Opposition's 18–27% premium is cost of covering same service the most expensive way, hiring or overtime, not restructuring.
Sequencing and measurement are already in the motion; refusing to pass it means the hard case never gets modelled.
Pilots excluded hospitals, transport and care homes, the sectors a national standard would bind hardest.
Fewer than half of pilot firms measured output consistently; managers absorbed coordination slack, redistributing gains.
Nine continuous-coverage operations needed 18–27% more staffed hours to hold service constant.
Two of nine clawed back part of the premium; seven didn't measure, so net cost is low-to-mid double digits of payroll.
Asymmetry: measured cost in hard sectors versus unmeasured saving in easy sectors; sequence, exempt, mandate measurement first.

verdict.keyDisagreement: Whether a nationwide four-day default should be legislated now with sequencing and exemptions, or delayed until continuous-coverage sectors are modelled and measured.
verdict.rationale: Both sides scored strongly on evidence and rebuttal, but the Opposition's clarity and persuasion edge reflected a tighter ledger: it granted the wellbeing findings while pressing the unmeasured cost in exactly the sectors the motion binds.
